title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about referencing: naming your sources so a reader can judge your work and trace every claim back to where it came from. If you are starting out at university, this might be one of the first academic skills that feels unfamiliar. It is also one of the most practical: get it right from the beginning and you save yourself a great deal of trouble later.

By the end of this course you will be able to explain why sources are named, describe what a reference needs, and spot and correct an inconsistent citation. You will also be able to identify and explain the sources in your own work, and build the habit of logging a source the moment you choose it, so your record stays organised and traceable.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Explain why academic work names its sources, and how that lets a reader judge your work and trace your claims.
  • Describe what a reference needs, and keep every citation in one consistent style.
  • Identify inconsistent citations in a piece of writing, and correct them to one consistent style.
  • Identify the sources in a piece of work, and explain to someone unfamiliar with it why they were selected and acknowledged.
  • Explain why recording a source as soon as you select it, rather than afterwards, keeps every citation traceable and organised.
  • Keep an organised, traceable record of your sources while you gather evidence, so each one can be found and checked again later.

title: In real academic practice
body: Referencing is not an exam skill that disappears after this course. Every essay, report and dissertation you write from now on will ask you to name your sources accurately and consistently, and markers notice straight away when a reference list does not match what is cited in the text. Get the habit right now, while the stakes are low, and it becomes automatic long before it matters for a big piece of work.

title: Signpost
body: The course has six short lessons. First, why sources are named at all. Second, what a reference needs and why one consistent style matters. Third, spotting and fixing citations that do not match your reference list. Fourth, identifying the sources in your own work and explaining why you acknowledged them. Fifth, why a source is logged the moment you select it, not afterwards. Sixth, keeping an organised source log as you gather evidence. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
instruction: Work through the six lessons in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: Every piece of academic work you read, and every piece you write, makes claims: a fact, a figure, an argument someone else first put forward. Academic writing names where each of these claims came from. This lesson looks at why, and at what naming a source actually does for the person reading your work.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage, the aim is to see clearly why sources are named at all, before you worry about the detail of how. Once the reason is clear, the rules for doing it make a great deal more sense.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • explain why academic work names its sources
  • identify what naming a source lets a reader do
  • trace a claim in a piece of writing back to where it came from

title: Concept: definition
body: To name a source is to tell the reader exactly where a claim, a fact or an idea came from. This is often called referencing or citing. It is not a formality added at the end of an essay. It is how a reader can tell the difference between what you worked out yourself and what you are drawing on from elsewhere, and how they can go back and check it.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have seen why sources get named and what that lets a reader do. The activities ahead let you practise spotting and using that reasoning; the check at the end asks you to apply it directly.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think of a recent piece of work you wrote. Did every claim that was not your own have a source named next to it? What made that easy, or difficult, to keep track of?

No right answers apply here; the aim is simply to notice your own habits.

title: Summary
body: You can now explain why academic work names its sources, identify what that naming lets a reader do, and trace a claim in a piece of writing back to where it came from. The next lesson looks at keeping that naming consistent, in one style, throughout a piece of work.

_items.title: See page 188 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: The last lesson looked at why sources are named at all. This lesson looks at what a reference itself needs to contain, and why every reference in a piece of work should follow the same style.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage, the aim is to recognise the parts a reference needs and to tell a consistent style from an inconsistent one. Memorising the exact punctuation of a particular style comes later.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • describe the elements a reference needs
  • classify a set of references by citation style
  • explain why one consistent style lets a reader trace every claim

title: Concept: definition
body: A reference is a short, structured description of a source: enough detail for a reader to find the exact thing you used. A citation style is a fixed way of ordering and punctuating that detail, so every reference in a piece of work looks the same and a reader always knows where to find each part.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have seen what a reference needs to contain and why one consistent style matters. The activities ahead let you practise spotting the elements and spotting inconsistency; the check at the end asks you to apply both.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Look at a reference list you have written recently, or one from something you have read. Is every entry in the same style? What would make it easier to keep that consistent next time?

No right answers apply here; the aim is simply to notice your own habits.

title: Summary
body: You can now describe the elements a reference needs, classify references by citation style, and explain why one consistent style lets a reader trace every claim. The next lesson looks at spotting and correcting a citation that breaks that consistency.

_items.title: See pages 188 to 189 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: The last lesson looked at what a reference needs and why one style should run through every entry. This lesson looks at the other half of the pairing: the citation in your text, and what happens when it stops matching its reference.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage, the aim is to notice when a citation and its reference-list entry have drifted apart, and to put that right. You are not expected to memorise every style's exact punctuation yet.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • identify an inconsistent citation in a piece of writing
  • locate the matching reference-list entry for a citation
  • correct an inconsistent citation to match one style

title: Concept: definition
body: A citation is inconsistent when it does not match its reference-list entry: the name is spelled differently, the year has changed, the format has switched from numbered to author-date, or the citation points to no entry at all. Every citation in a piece of work should lead a reader to exactly one entry, in the same style throughout.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have seen what makes a citation inconsistent with its reference. The activities ahead let you practise spotting a mismatch and finding its entry; the check at the end asks you to apply both to correct one.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Pick a piece of writing you have cited sources in before. Choose three citations at random and check each one against its reference-list entry. Did any of them not quite match?

No right answers apply here; the aim is simply to notice how easily a mismatch can creep in.

title: Summary
body: You can now identify an inconsistent citation, locate its matching reference-list entry, and correct a citation so it matches one style. The next lesson looks at identifying and explaining the sources used in your own work.

_items.title: See pages 189 to 191 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: The last lesson looked at catching a citation that has drifted from its reference. This lesson turns to your own writing: finding every source you have actually drawn on, and being ready to say why each one earned its place.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage, the aim is to spot every source your own draft depends on, including the ones you have not directly quoted, and to put together a reference entry for each in a consistent format.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • identify the sources used in a piece of work
  • assemble a reference entry in a consistent format
  • explain to a newcomer why a source was acknowledged

title: Concept: definition
body: A source is used in a piece of work whenever it contributes a quote, a paraphrased idea, a statistic, or a line of reasoning, whether or not its wording appears directly. Identifying your sources means going back through a draft and listing everything it has actually drawn on, not just what has been quoted.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have seen what counts as using a source and what a reference entry needs. The activities ahead let you practise spotting a source's use and assembling its entry; the check at the end asks you to apply both.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Look back at something you have written recently. Pick one idea, statistic, or line of reasoning that came from somewhere else. Could you say exactly which source it came from, and why you used it?

No right answers apply here; the aim is simply to notice how easily a source's contribution can go unacknowledged.

title: Summary
body: You can now identify the sources used in a piece of work, assemble a reference entry in a consistent format, and explain to a newcomer why a source was acknowledged. The next lesson looks at building the habit of logging a source the moment you choose it.

_items.title: See pages 195 to 198 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: The last lesson looked at finding every source your own work depends on. This lesson looks at when to record that detail: the moment you select a source, not whenever you get round to it.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage, the aim is to see why logging a source immediately matters, and what a traceable record of it actually needs to contain.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • explain why a source is logged at the point it is selected
  • recognise the risk of logging a source after the fact
  • describe what a traceable source record contains

title: Concept: definition
body: Logging a source means recording the detail you will need to cite it, at the moment you decide to use it: the reference itself, where you found it, and the exact page or location the idea came from. Done immediately, this detail is accurate. Left until later, it has to be reconstructed from memory.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have seen why logging a source immediately matters and what a record needs to contain. The activities ahead let you practise spotting the risk of delay and the steps of logging well; the check at the end asks you to apply both.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think about the last piece of work you researched. Did you log each source as you found it, or try to reconstruct the details afterward? How did that go?

No right answers apply here; the aim is simply to notice your own timing.

title: Summary
body: You can now explain why a source is logged at the point it is selected, recognise the risk of logging one after the fact, and describe what a traceable source record contains. The next lesson looks at organising that log while you gather evidence.

title: Orientation
body: The last lesson looked at logging a source the moment you select it. This lesson looks at keeping that log organised, so every entry stays easy to find again while you keep gathering evidence.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage, the aim is to keep a source log running as you work, organise it so an entry can be found again, and check an entry against its original source.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • keep a source log while gathering evidence
  • organise a source log so an entry can be found again
  • check a source log entry against its original source

title: Concept: definition
body: A source log is a running record of every source used, built up as you gather evidence rather than assembled at the end. Keeping it organised means each entry can be found again quickly, by topic, by source type, or in the order it was added; checking it means comparing an entry back against the original source to confirm nothing has drifted.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have seen what keeps a source log usable: adding to it as you go, organising it, and checking entries against their originals. The activities ahead let you practise organising and checking; the check at the end asks you to apply both.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Look at how you currently keep track of sources, if you keep track at all. Could you find a specific entry again quickly? When did you last check one against the original?

No right answers apply here; the aim is simply to notice how your own log holds up.

title: Summary
body: You can now keep a source log while gathering evidence, organise it so an entry can be found again, and check an entry against its original source. This closes the course's coverage of giving every source the record it needs.

title: Assessment introduction
body:
This is the test for the whole course. It covers everything you've studied in the lessons, with a set of questions to work through.

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Naming your sources, building a reference, and keeping everything in one consistent style are no longer unfamiliar: you now have a first, solid foundation in referencing. You can explain why sources are named, describe what a reference needs, spot and correct an inconsistent citation, identify and explain the sources in your own work, and keep an organised, traceable log of sources as you gather them. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: Start using what you've learned in the very next piece of work you submit: log each source as you choose it, check your reference list matches what you've cited in the text, and keep everything in one consistent style from the first draft. You will also use this habit of logging sources as you go when you come to finding and using sources for a longer piece of work.

title: Where this goes next
body: This is the first course in the Referencing pathway. The natural next step is the intermediate course, which moves from getting referencing right to judging it: checking a paraphrase against its source, weighing whether a reference list's range reflects real research, and handling source types that do not fit a standard template. The habit of logging a source as you select it, which you have just built, is exactly what makes that judgement possible later.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 188 to 198 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

body: Why does academic work name its sources?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does academic work name its sources?

_items.text: So a reader can judge the quality of a source and trace a claim back to it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Naming a source lets a reader judge it and follow a claim back to where it came from.

_items.text: So the writer avoids being accused of using too few sources in the work.
_items.feedback: The point is traceability for the reader, not defending how many sources were used.

_items.text: So the reference list looks longer and more thorough to whoever marks it.
_items.feedback: A reference list exists for traceability, not to look impressively long.

_items.text: So other students can find extra reading on the same topic later.
_items.feedback: That can happen, but it is not why academic work names its sources.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Naming a source lets a reader judge the quality of what you used and trace any claim back to its origin.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reader can do once they know where a claim came from.

body: What does a reference need to let a reader trace a claim back to its source?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does a reference need to let a reader trace a claim?

_items.text: Enough detail, in one consistent format, to let a reader locate the exact source used.
_items.feedback: Yes. Enough detail in one consistent format is what lets a reader find the exact source.

_items.text: A description of the source and where the writer first came across it in general terms.
_items.feedback: That describes a note to self, not a reference that lets a reader locate the source.

_items.text: A short paraphrase of the source's whole argument, explained in the writer's own words.
_items.feedback: A paraphrase helps in the text, but a reference needs locating detail, not a summary.

_items.text: The source's title and type, formatted however suits the writer's personal preference.
_items.feedback: Any format can work, but only if it is applied consistently; personal preference is not the test.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Enough detail, in one consistent format, is what lets a reader locate the exact source.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reader actually needs in order to find the source themselves.

body: What makes a citation inconsistent with a piece of writing's reference list?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What makes a citation inconsistent with the reference list?

_items.text: It doesn't match the format or details recorded for that source in the reference list.
_items.feedback: Yes. A citation is inconsistent when it doesn't match that source's own reference-list entry.

_items.text: It cites a source that the marker would personally disagree with.
_items.feedback: Inconsistency is about matching format and detail, not about agreeing with a source's content.

_items.text: It appears more times across the essay than other citations do.
_items.feedback: How often a source is cited doesn't make a citation inconsistent.

_items.text: It sits at the end of a sentence rather than at the start.
_items.feedback: Where a citation sits in the sentence doesn't make it inconsistent.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A citation is inconsistent when it doesn't match the format and detail recorded for that source elsewhere.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Compare the citation against its own entry in the reference list.

body: Why might you need to explain the sources in your own work to someone unfamiliar with it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why explain your sources to someone unfamiliar with the work?

_items.text: So they can see why each source was selected and how it supports the work.
_items.feedback: Yes. Explaining your sources shows why you chose and acknowledged each one.

_items.text: So they can check that you remembered to cite every source you read.
_items.feedback: That checks completeness, not why a source was selected and acknowledged.

_items.text: So they can judge whether you read enough sources overall for the task.
_items.feedback: That judges quantity, not the reasoning behind choosing and acknowledging each source.

_items.text: So they can confirm the sources are recent enough to be acceptable.
_items.feedback: Recency is one possible reason among several, not the purpose of the explanation itself.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Explaining your sources lets someone see why each one was selected and acknowledged.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the explanation actually reveals about your choices.

body: Why record a source the moment you select it, rather than afterwards?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why record a source as soon as you select it?

_items.text: Because the details are accurate and complete only while the source is still in front of you.
_items.feedback: Yes. The details are easiest to get right while the source is still in front of you.

_items.text: Because referencing software works faster when sources are logged immediately.
_items.feedback: Software speed isn't the reason; accuracy while the source is at hand is.

_items.text: Because markers expect to see a timestamp on every source you log.
_items.feedback: Markers don't check timestamps; the reason is accuracy, not an expectation to meet.

_items.text: Because recording it later would mean citing the source twice by mistake.
_items.feedback: Logging late risks losing detail, not duplicating the citation itself.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Recording a source while it's in front of you keeps the details accurate and complete.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you risk losing if you wait until later.

body: What makes a source log useful while you are gathering evidence for a task?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What makes a source log useful while gathering evidence?

_items.text: It is organised so each entry can be found and checked again later.
_items.feedback: Yes. An organised log lets you find and check each entry again later.

_items.text: It lists every source in the exact order you happened to read them.
_items.feedback: Reading order doesn't make a log traceable; organisation for retrieval does.

_items.text: It contains only the sources you already expect to use in the final piece.
_items.feedback: Pre-filtering sources isn't the point; keeping every entry traceable is.

_items.text: It is kept separately until the writing stage, when it gets tidied up.
_items.feedback: Leaving it until later is exactly the risk a source log is meant to avoid.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An organised log lets you find and check each source again later, whenever you need to.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you need to be able to do with the log afterwards.

title: Activity: what naming a source lets a reader do
displayTitle: Match what you do to what it lets a reader do
body: Three things you might do when using a source, and three things that doing them lets a reader do.
instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Match each action to what it lets a reader do.

_items.text: You give the exact page number for a statistic you quote.

_options.text: Check the claim against its original source
Tell your thinking from someone else's
Find further reading on the topic

_items.text: You put quotation marks around a sentence you copied and name its author.

_options.text: Check the claim against its original source
Tell your thinking from someone else's
Find further reading on the topic

_items.text: You list the full reference for the study that first introduced an idea you describe.

_options.text: Check the claim against its original source
Tell your thinking from someone else's
Find further reading on the topic

_feedback.correct: That's right. Each action lets a reader do something different: check a figure, tell your thinking from someone else's, or read further.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the reader can actually do once they see that marker, not just that a marker is there.

title: Activity: tracing a claim
displayTitle: Put these steps in order
body: These are the steps a reader follows once a source has been named. They are out of order.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the four steps a reader follows to trace a claim back to its source in order, from first to last.

_items.text: The reader spots the reference marker next to your claim.
The reader looks up the matching entry in your reference list.
The reader locates the original source itself.
The reader checks your claim against what the source actually says.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order. The marker points to the reference list entry, which points to the source itself, which the reader can then check your claim against.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. Think about what the reader needs to find before they can do the next step. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some steps are in the right place, but not all. Each step depends on the one before it. Try again.

title: Worked example: naming a source
displayTitle: Worked example: naming a source
body:
Two students each use the same statistic in their coursework.

{{learner-a}} writes: ‘Over sixty per cent of first-year students report feeling unprepared for independent study.’ No source is given. A reader has no way of checking where this figure came from, or whether it is reliable.

{{learner-b}} writes the same figure, but names the study it came from and gives a reference. A reader can now trace the claim straight back to its origin, see the sample it was based on, and judge for {{learner-b-possessive-pronoun}} own self how much weight to give it.

Only {{learner-b}}'s version lets a reader do anything with the claim beyond simply taking it on trust.

back.body: Go back to the original and see whether your claim is a fair account of what it says.

title: Activity: common ways a source gets named
displayTitle: Common ways you will see a source named
body: Four common ways a source is named in a piece of academic work. Open each to see it explained.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: An in-text citation
_items.body: A short marker next to the claim itself, such as a name and year, pointing to the full entry in your reference list.

_items.title: A reference list entry
_items.body: The full publication details for a source, listed at the end of your work in a single consistent style.

_items.title: A footnote
_items.body: Some subjects place the source detail at the bottom of the page instead of in a reference list; the reader still ends up at the same information.

_items.title: A direct quotation marker
_items.body: Quotation marks around copied wording show exactly which words are someone else's, as well as whose they are.

title: Practical guidance: before you submit

body: Run through this list before you submit a piece of work in {{context}}.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Every statistic, fact or idea that is not your own has a source named next to it.

Every reference list entry has enough detail for someone else to find the original.
Quotation marks are around any wording you copied directly.
You have used one consistent style throughout.

title: Check 1: why sources are named
displayTitle: Which of these best explains why academic work names its sources?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these best explains why academic work names its sources?

_items.text: So a reader can tell what you worked out yourself from what you are drawing on from elsewhere, and check it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Naming a source lets a reader separate your own thinking from what you have drawn on elsewhere, and go back and check it.

_items.text: So the essay reaches the expected word count.
_items.feedback: Word count is not the reason sources are named.

_items.text: Because a lecturer marks it down if sources are missing, regardless of the reason.
_items.feedback: A marking habit is not the underlying reason; it exists because of what naming a source lets a reader do.

_items.text: So the essay looks more impressive to a reader.
_items.feedback: Appearance is not the reason sources are named.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Naming a source lets a reader tell your own thinking from what you drew on elsewhere, and check the claim for themselves.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what naming a source actually lets a reader do with your claim.
_incorrect.final: Naming a source lets a reader tell your own thinking from what you drew on elsewhere, and check the claim for themselves. Word count, marking habit and appearance are not the reason.

title: Check 2: what a missing source costs a reader
displayTitle: A classmate reads your essay and finds a claim with no source given. What can they NOT do, that they could do if a source had been named?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What can a reader not do when a claim has no source named?

_items.text: Go back and check whether the claim is an accurate account of where it came from.
_items.feedback: Right. Without a source, a reader cannot trace the claim back and check it.

_items.text: Understand the sentence grammatically.
_items.feedback: A missing source does not stop a reader understanding the sentence itself.

_items.text: Finish reading the essay.
_items.feedback: A missing source does not stop a reader continuing to read.

_items.text: See that the sentence is about referencing.
_items.feedback: This is not what a missing source prevents.

_feedback.correct: Right. Without a source, a reader cannot trace the claim back and check it; everything else in the sentence is still perfectly readable.

_incorrect.notFinal: Look again at what a missing source specifically stops a reader doing, not at the sentence in general.
_incorrect.final: A missing source stops a reader tracing the claim back to check it. It does not stop them reading or understanding the sentence.

title: Check 3: tracing a claim
displayTitle: You are reading a piece of work in {{context}} and want to trace a claim back to where it came from. Which piece of information do you need?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which piece of information lets you trace a claim back to its source?

_items.text: The reference marker next to the claim, and the matching entry in the reference list.
_items.feedback: Yes. The marker points you to the reference list entry, which is what lets you trace the claim to its origin.

_items.text: The word count of the piece of work.
_items.feedback: Word count does not point you to a claim's source.

_items.text: The date the piece of work was submitted.
_items.feedback: A submission date does not point you to a claim's source.

_items.text: The font and formatting used in the piece of work.
_items.feedback: Formatting does not point you to a claim's source.

_feedback.correct: Yes. The reference marker and its matching reference list entry are what let you trace a claim back to its source.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about which detail actually points you back to where a claim came from.
_incorrect.final: The reference marker and its matching reference list entry are what let you trace a claim back to its source; word count, date and formatting do not.

title: Activity: elements of a reference
displayTitle: Turn each card over
body: Four parts a reference usually needs. Select a card to flip it and see what it tells the reader.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over.

back.body: Tells the reader who is responsible for the idea or the data.
Tells the reader when the source was published, which matters if newer work has since changed the picture.
Tells the reader exactly which piece of work this is, out of everything that author has written.
Tells the reader where to go to find the work itself.

title: Activity: classify by citation style
displayTitle: Match each reference to its style

instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Match each reference entry to its citation style.

_items.text: Dennis, A. and Abbott, J. (2026) Excelling at University. London: Routledge.

_options.text: Harvard style (author-date)
Numbered style
Footnote style

Numbered style
Footnote style

_options.text: Harvard style (author-date)
Numbered style
Footnote style

_feedback.correct: That's right. Harvard style leads with the author and year, numbered style marks the position in a numbered list, and footnote style places a number at the point of use.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at where the author's name and the number, if there is one, sit in each entry.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some of these are right, but not all. Check the rest.

title: Worked example: one style, every reference
displayTitle: Worked example: one style, every reference
body:
Two students each produce a reference list for the same essay.

{{learner-a}} copies each reference straight from wherever it was found: one entry in Harvard style, the next numbered, the next with the year in a different place again. Every entry has the right information somewhere, but a reader has to work out the pattern afresh each time.

{{learner-b}} rewrites every entry into the same style before submitting. A reader can now predict exactly where the author, year and title will sit in any entry, and trace a claim to its reference without having to puzzle over the format first.

The information in both lists is complete. Only {{learner-b}}'s list lets a reader use it quickly and reliably.

title: Activity: building a reference in order
displayTitle: Put the parts of this reference in order
body: These are the parts of a single Harvard-style reference. They are out of order.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the four parts of a Harvard-style reference in the correct order.

_items.text: Author: Dennis, A. and Abbott, J.
Title: Excelling at University.
Place and publisher: London: Routledge.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order for Harvard style: author, year, title, then place and publisher.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. Harvard style always leads with who wrote it, then when. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some parts are in the right place, but not all. Try again.

title: Activity: why one style, not several
displayTitle: Why one style, not several
body: Four reasons a piece of work sticks to one citation style throughout. Open each to see it explained.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: A reader learns the pattern once
_items.body: Once a reader knows where the author and year sit in one entry, they know where to find them in every other entry too.

_items.title: Mixed styles slow a reader down
_items.body: A reader who meets a different layout in every entry has to re-work out the pattern each time, instead of reading for content.

_items.title: It signals care
_items.body: A consistent reference list suggests the same attention was given to the sources as to the argument built on them.

_items.title: It matches what is expected
_items.body: Most subjects and institutions expect one named style throughout a piece of work, not a mixture.

title: Practical guidance: one style, every reference
displayTitle: Before you submit work in {{context}}
body: Run through this list before you submit a reference list.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Every entry gives the author, the year, the title, and where the source can be found.
Every entry follows the same citation style as every other entry.
The punctuation and ordering look the same across entries, not just the content.
You have checked your subject's or institution's expected style before choosing one.

title: Check 1: elements of a reference
displayTitle: Which of these is a core element every reference needs?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these is a core element every reference needs?

_items.text: The author, so a reader knows who is responsible for the idea.
_items.feedback: Yes. The author is one of the core elements a reference needs.

_items.text: The exact font used in the original source.
_items.feedback: Formatting detail like font is not something a reference records.

_items.text: The student's own opinion of the source.
_items.feedback: A reference records where a source is from, not a reader's opinion of it.

_items.text: The number of times the source has been cited elsewhere.
_items.feedback: Citation counts are not part of a reference entry.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The author is a core element; font, opinion and citation counts are not part of a reference entry.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reference needs in order for a reader to find the exact source.
_incorrect.final: The author is a core element every reference needs. Font, personal opinion and citation counts are not.

title: Check 2: cost of mixed styles
displayTitle: Two reference-list entries in the same list use different citation styles, one Harvard, one numbered. What problem does this cause a reader?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What problem does mixing citation styles in one reference list cause a reader?

_items.text: The reader cannot predict where to find the same kind of information in each entry.
_items.feedback: Right. Without one consistent style, the reader has to re-work out the pattern for every entry.

_items.text: The references take up more space on the page.
_items.feedback: Page space is not the problem mixed styles cause.

_items.text: The references no longer sit in alphabetical order.
_items.feedback: Alphabetical order is a separate matter from citation style.

_items.text: The essay's word count goes up.
_items.feedback: Reference list entries do not affect an essay's word count in this way.

_feedback.correct: Right. Mixed styles force a reader to re-work out the pattern for every entry, instead of reading for content.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what a reader has to redo every time the layout changes.
_incorrect.final: Mixed styles stop a reader predicting where information sits in each entry. Page space, alphabetical order and word count are not the issue.

title: Check 3: what one style lets a reader do
displayTitle: In a piece of work for {{context}}, every reference list entry follows the same style. What does this let a reader do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does a consistent citation style let a reader do?

_items.text: Trace any claim back to its source using the same pattern every time.
_items.feedback: Yes. One consistent style means a reader can trace every claim the same way, without re-learning the pattern.

_items.text: Finish reading faster.
_items.feedback: Reading speed is not what a consistent style is for.

_items.text: Avoid using quotation marks.
_items.feedback: Quotation marks are a separate convention from citation style.

_items.text: Skip the reference list entirely.
_items.feedback: A consistent style does not remove the need for a reference list.

_feedback.correct: Yes. One consistent style lets a reader trace any claim the same way, every time.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what staying consistent specifically lets a reader do when tracing a claim.
_incorrect.final: A consistent style lets a reader trace any claim back to its source the same way every time. It is not about reading speed, quotation marks, or skipping the list.

title: Activity: consistent or inconsistent
displayTitle: Classify each citation
body: Three in-text citations, each checked against the reference list it should match.
instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Classify each citation as consistent or inconsistent with its reference-list entry.

_items.text: Text cites (Dennis and Abbott, 2026). Reference list has Dennis, A. and Abbott, J. (2026).

_options.text: Consistent
Inconsistent

_items.text: Text cites (Dennis and Abbott, 2024). Reference list has Dennis, A. and Abbott, J. (2026).

_options.text: Consistent
Inconsistent

_items.text: Text cites [3]. Reference list has no entry numbered 3.

_options.text: Consistent
Inconsistent

_feedback.correct: That's right. A citation is only consistent when its name, year or number matches the reference-list entry exactly.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Check the year and the name against the reference list entry, and check the number actually exists.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some of these are right, but not all. Check the rest.

title: Activity: find the matching entry
displayTitle: Match each citation to its reference
body: Three in-text citations. Match each one to the reference-list entry it should point to.
instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Match each citation to its reference-list entry.

_items.text: (Dennis and Abbott, 2026)

_options.text: Dennis, A. and Abbott, J. (2026) Excelling at University. London: Routledge.
Okafor, R. (2025) Study Skills for the Sciences. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

_items.text: (Okafor, 2025)

_options.text: Dennis, A. and Abbott, J. (2026) Excelling at University. London: Routledge.
Okafor, R. (2025) Study Skills for the Sciences. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Each citation's name and year point to exactly one reference-list entry.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Match the author name and year in the citation to the author name and year in the entry.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: One of these is right, but not both. Check the other.

title: Worked example: fixing an inconsistent citation
displayTitle: Worked example: fixing an inconsistent citation
body:
Two students each notice a citation that looks slightly off before submitting.

{{learner-a}} sees that the in-text citation reads (Dennis, 2025) but the reference list has Dennis, A. and Abbott, J. (2026). {{learner-a-pronoun}} leaves it as it is, assuming it is close enough.

{{learner-b}} notices the same mismatch, checks the reference list, and corrects the citation to (Dennis and Abbott, 2026) so it leads a reader to exactly the entry it should.

Only {{learner-b}}'s citation now does what a citation is for: taking a reader straight to the right source, with no guessing.

title: Activity: steps to correct a citation
displayTitle: Put these steps in order
body: These are the steps for correcting an inconsistent citation. They are out of order.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the steps for correcting an inconsistent citation in the correct order.

_items.text: Find the citation's matching entry in the reference list.
Compare the name, year and any number against the citation.
Note exactly which part does not match.
Rewrite the citation so it matches the reference-list entry.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order: find the entry first, compare the detail, note the mismatch, then correct the citation to match.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. You need to find the entry before you can compare it. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some steps are in the right place, but not all. Try again.

title: Activity: how a mismatch creeps in
displayTitle: How a mismatch creeps in
body: Four common ways a citation stops matching its reference. Open each to see it explained.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: A reference is edited later, the citation is not
_items.body: The reference list gets a correction, but every citation pointing to it in the text is left as it was.

_items.title: A source is swapped for another
_items.body: A different edition or a different source is used, but the old citation stays in the text.

_items.title: A name is typed differently each time
_items.body: An author's name is spelled or ordered one way in the text and another way in the reference list.

_items.title: A numbered citation outlives its number
_items.body: An entry is added or removed from a numbered list, but the numbers already used in the text are not renumbered to match.

title: Practical guidance: checking citations against references
displayTitle: Before you submit work in {{context}}
body: Run through this list before you submit a piece of writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Every citation in the text has a matching entry in the reference list.
The name and year in each citation match the name and year in its entry exactly.
Every numbered citation points to a number that still exists in the list.
No reference-list entry has been edited without checking the citations that point to it.

title: Check 1: spotting an inconsistent citation
displayTitle: A citation reads (Okafor, 2024). The reference list has Okafor, R. (2025). What is this an example of?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does a mismatched year between a citation and its reference-list entry show?

_items.text: An inconsistent citation, because the year does not match the reference-list entry.
_items.feedback: Yes. A mismatched year is exactly the kind of inconsistency to catch and correct.

_items.text: Two separate sources by the same author.
_items.feedback: Only one entry appears here, so this is not two sources.

_items.text: A missing reference, because no year is given in the text.
_items.feedback: A year is given in the citation; it is simply the wrong one.

_items.text: A correctly formatted citation.
_items.feedback: The year does not match its entry, so this citation is not correct as it stands.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A mismatched year between a citation and its entry is an inconsistent citation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Compare the year given in the citation with the year on the reference-list entry.
_incorrect.final: The year in the citation does not match the entry, which makes this an inconsistent citation, not a second source, a missing reference, or a correct one.

title: Check 2: finding the entry
displayTitle: A citation reads [5], but the reference list has no entry numbered 5. What should happen next?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should happen when a numbered citation points to no entry in the reference list?

_items.text: The source the citation refers to should be identified and either given the right number or added to the list.
_items.feedback: Right. A citation with no matching entry needs the correct entry locating or adding, not leaving as it is.

_items.text: The citation should be deleted from the text, but the sentence left as it is.
_items.feedback: Deleting the citation without fixing the claim leaves an unsupported statement.

_items.text: The number should be left as it is; readers can work it out.
_items.feedback: A citation that points to nothing cannot be traced by a reader, however carefully they look.

_items.text: The whole reference list should be renumbered from scratch.
_items.feedback: A single missing entry does not require renumbering every entry in the list.

_feedback.correct: Right. The missing entry needs locating and adding or correctly numbering, so the citation leads somewhere.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what a reader needs the citation to do: lead them to a real entry.
_incorrect.final: The source needs locating and the entry adding or correctly numbering. Deleting the citation, leaving it, or renumbering everything does not fix the underlying problem.

title: Check 3: correcting a citation
displayTitle: In a piece of work for {{context}}, a citation reads (Dennis, 2026) but the entry is Dennis, A. and Abbott, J. (2026). What correction is needed?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What correction does a citation missing a co-author need?

_items.text: Add the second author, so the citation reads (Dennis and Abbott, 2026).
_items.feedback: Yes. The citation should name both authors shown on the reference-list entry.

_items.text: Change the year to the year the work was cited, not published.
_items.feedback: The year in a citation reflects the source's publication date, not when it was used.

_items.text: Remove the citation, since one author's name is already given.
_items.feedback: Removing the citation would leave the claim unsupported; the fix is to complete it, not delete it.

_items.text: Leave it as it is; one author's name is close enough.
_items.feedback: A citation should match its entry exactly, not approximately.

_feedback.correct: Yes. The citation should be corrected to name both authors, matching the reference-list entry exactly.

_incorrect.notFinal: Compare the citation to the full reference-list entry and see what it is missing.
_incorrect.final: The citation should name both authors, matching the entry exactly. The year, deletion, and approximate matches are not the fix.

title: Activity: needs a citation or not
displayTitle: Classify each sentence
body: Three sentences from a short piece of work.
instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Classify each sentence as needing a citation or not.

_items.text: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.

_options.text: Needs a citation
Does not need one

_items.text: Dennis and Abbott (2026) found that students who logged sources as they wrote cited more accurately than those who added references afterwards.

_options.text: Needs a citation
Does not need one

_items.text: This idea builds on the method Okafor (2025) describes, applied here to a different subject.

_options.text: Needs a citation
Does not need one

_feedback.correct: That's right. A borrowed finding or method needs a citation, even if it is not quoted directly; a widely known fact does not.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Ask whether the claim is common knowledge or whether it depends on someone else's work.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some of these are right, but not all. Check the rest.

title: Activity: assembling a journal-article reference
displayTitle: Put the parts of this reference in order
body: These are the parts of a single Harvard-style journal-article reference. They are out of order.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the parts of a Harvard-style journal-article reference in the correct order.

_items.text: Author: Okafor, R.
Article title: 'Logging sources while you write'
Journal, volume and pages: Study Skills Review, 12(3), pp. 44-52

_feedback.correct: That is the right order for a Harvard-style journal-article reference: author, year, article title, then journal with volume and pages.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. Harvard style always leads with who wrote it, then when. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some parts are in the right place, but not all. Try again.

title: Worked example: finding every source
displayTitle: Worked example: finding every source
body:
Two students each review their own draft before submitting.

{{learner-a}} lists only the sources {{learner-a-pronoun}} quoted directly. A statistic borrowed from a report, and an argument structure adapted from another author, are left off the list because neither was quoted word for word.

{{learner-b}} goes back through the draft sentence by sentence, listing every source that contributed a quote, a statistic, or an idea, whether or not the wording was copied directly.

Only {{learner-b}}'s reference list reflects everything the draft actually depends on.

title: Activity: why a source earns its place
displayTitle: Turn each card over
body: Four reasons a source is acknowledged in a piece of work. Select a card to flip it and see the reason explained.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over.

back.body: It gives credit to the person whose idea, data or wording is being used.
It lets a reader go and check the claim against the original source.
It shows clearly which parts of the work are the writer's own thinking and which are borrowed.
It shows the writer has engaged with existing work on the topic, not just their own view.

title: Activity: ways a source gets used
displayTitle: Ways a source gets used
body: Four ways a source can contribute to a piece of work, all of which need acknowledging. Open each to see it explained.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: A direct quote
_items.body: The source's exact words are used, inside quotation marks.

_items.title: A paraphrase
_items.body: The source's idea is put into the writer's own words, but the idea itself still came from the source.

_items.title: A statistic or finding
_items.body: A number, result or finding from the source is used to support a claim.

_items.title: A line of reasoning
_items.body: The source's argument or structure is followed or adapted, even without quoting any of it directly.

title: Practical guidance: finding every source in a draft
displayTitle: Before you submit work in {{context}}
body: Run through this list before you submit a piece of writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: You have gone through the draft sentence by sentence, not just checked the quotes.
Every borrowed idea, statistic or line of reasoning has a source attached, even if it was paraphrased.
Each source has a complete reference entry in your chosen style.
You could explain, for each source, exactly why it was used.

title: Check 1: identifying a used source
displayTitle: A sentence paraphrases an idea from a report, without a direct quote. Does this source need acknowledging?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Does a paraphrased idea need its source acknowledged?

_items.text: Yes, because the idea still came from the report, even though the wording did not.
_items.feedback: Yes. Paraphrasing an idea still means the idea came from that source, so it needs acknowledging.

_items.text: No, because nothing was quoted directly.
_items.feedback: Acknowledging a source is not limited to direct quotes; a paraphrased idea still needs its source named.

_items.text: No, because the writer rephrased it in their own words.
_items.feedback: Rephrasing changes the wording, not where the idea came from.

_items.text: Only if the report is well known.
_items.feedback: How well known a source is does not change whether it needs acknowledging.

_feedback.correct: Yes. A paraphrased idea still came from its source, so it needs acknowledging regardless of wording.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about where the idea originated, not just how it is worded now.
_incorrect.final: A paraphrased idea still needs acknowledging; what matters is where the idea came from, not the exact wording, how well known the source is, or whether it was rephrased.

title: Check 2: assembling a reference entry
displayTitle: A journal-article reference is missing its volume and page numbers. What is wrong with the entry?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is missing from an incomplete journal-article reference?

_items.text: A reader cannot locate the exact article within the journal issue.
_items.feedback: Right. Without volume and page numbers, a reader cannot find the exact article, even with the author and title.

_items.text: The article's claims become less trustworthy.
_items.feedback: Missing locator detail affects findability, not the trustworthiness of the claims themselves.

_items.text: The citation style automatically switches to numbered.
_items.feedback: Missing detail in one entry does not change the citation style being used.

_items.text: Nothing; author and title are enough.
_items.feedback: Author and title alone do not let a reader locate the article within its journal issue.

_feedback.correct: Right. Volume and page numbers let a reader locate the exact article within its journal issue.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what a reader still cannot do without the volume and pages.
_incorrect.final: Without volume and page numbers, a reader cannot locate the exact article. Trustworthiness, citation style and completeness without this detail are not the issue.

title: Check 3: explaining why a source was acknowledged
displayTitle: In a piece of work for {{context}}, a newcomer asks why you cited a source for an idea you put in your own words. What is the best explanation?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the best explanation for citing a paraphrased idea?

_items.text: The idea itself came from that source, even though the wording is mine.
_items.feedback: Yes. Citing credits where the idea came from, independent of whose words express it.

_items.text: It makes the piece of work look longer.
_items.feedback: Length is not the reason a source is acknowledged.

_items.text: It is required only when a direct quote is used.
_items.feedback: Acknowledging a source is not limited to direct quotes.

_items.text: It avoids having to explain the idea in your own words.
_items.feedback: Citing a source does not replace explaining the idea; it credits where the idea came from.

_feedback.correct: Yes. The citation credits where the idea came from, regardless of whose words express it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what a citation is actually crediting: the wording, or the origin of the idea.
_incorrect.final: A citation credits where the idea came from, not the wording used. Length, quote-only requirements, and avoiding explanation are not the reason.

title: Activity: logged now or logged later
displayTitle: Match each habit to its outcome
body: Two ways of recording a source, and what tends to happen as a result.
instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Match each source-logging habit to its likely outcome.

_items.text: The reference and page number are noted the moment the source is selected.

_options.text: The detail stays accurate and the source stays traceable.
The exact page is usually misremembered later.

_items.text: The source is read now but the reference is only written down a week later, from memory.

_options.text: The detail stays accurate and the source stays traceable.
The exact page is usually misremembered later.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Logging a source immediately keeps its detail accurate; delaying it leaves the detail to memory.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how reliable memory is for an exact page number days or weeks later.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: One of these is right, but not both. Check the other.

title: Activity: what a traceable record contains
displayTitle: Turn each card over
body: Four things a traceable source record needs. Select a card to flip it and see why.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over.

back.body: Author, year, title, and where the source can be found again.
The specific page, paragraph or timestamp the idea actually came from, not just the source as a whole.
A short note on which idea, quote or statistic this source supports, so its purpose is not forgotten.
For an online source especially, when it was found, in case the content there later changes.

title: Worked example: logging as you go
displayTitle: Worked example: logging as you go
body:
Two students each gather several sources over an afternoon of reading.

{{learner-a}} reads six sources, planning to write down the references once the reading is finished. By the end, {{learner-a-pronoun}} cannot remember which page two of the statistics came from.

{{learner-b}} notes the reference, the page, and what each source was used for the moment each one is selected, each time, before the next.

Only {{learner-b}}'s sources remain fully traceable once the reading is done.

title: Activity: logging a source at the point of selection
displayTitle: Put these steps in order
body: These are the steps for logging a source the moment you decide to use it. They are out of order.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the steps for logging a source at the point of selection in the correct order.

_items.text: Notice an idea, quote or statistic worth using.
Note the exact page or location it came from.
Note the full reference detail for the source.
Add a short note on what the source will be used for.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order: notice the idea first, then capture the exact location, the reference, and its purpose, all before moving on.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. The idea has to be noticed before anything about it can be logged. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some steps are in the right place, but not all. Try again.

title: Activity: why logging later goes wrong
displayTitle: Why logging later goes wrong
body: Four common ways delayed logging fails. Open each to see it explained.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: The exact page is forgotten
_items.body: A general sense of 'somewhere in that chapter' is not enough to point a reader to the right page.

_items.title: Two similar sources get confused
_items.body: When several sources are read together, which detail came from which one can blur.

_items.title: The source cannot be found again
_items.body: A webpage may change or disappear, leaving nothing to check the detail against later.

_items.title: The idea's original purpose is lost
_items.body: Without a note on why a source was selected, it is hard to remember what point it was meant to support.

title: Practical guidance: logging a source immediately
displayTitle: Each time you select a source in {{context}}
body: Run through this list the moment you decide to use a source.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: You have noted the full reference detail before moving on.
You have noted the exact page or location the idea came from.
You have written a short note on what you intend to use it for.
For an online source, you have noted the date you accessed it.

title: Check 1: why log immediately
displayTitle: Why is a source logged the moment it is selected, rather than afterward?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is a source logged the moment it is selected?

_items.text: Because the detail, especially the exact page, is accurate now and harder to recall correctly later.
_items.feedback: Yes. Detail noted at the time is accurate; detail reconstructed afterward depends on memory.

_items.text: Because it saves time at the end of the project.
_items.feedback: Logging as you go is about accuracy, not about saving time overall.

_items.text: Because a style guide requires it.
_items.feedback: No style guide dictates when you log a source; the reason is accuracy.

_items.text: Because sources found later in a project do not need logging.
_items.feedback: Every source used needs logging, regardless of when in the project it is found.

_feedback.correct: Yes. Logging immediately keeps the detail accurate, especially the exact page, which memory struggles to hold onto.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about how reliable memory is for an exact page number, days or weeks later.
_incorrect.final: Logging immediately keeps detail accurate, especially the exact page. It is not about saving time, a style-guide rule, or exempting later sources.

title: Check 2: recognising the risk
displayTitle: A student plans to write down every reference once their reading is finished for the week. What risk does this create?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What risk does delaying source logging create?

_items.text: Exact page numbers and which source supported which point may be misremembered or confused.
_items.feedback: Right. Delay risks exactly this kind of detail being misremembered or mixed up between sources.

_items.text: The sources will no longer count as valid.
_items.feedback: Timing of logging does not affect whether a source is valid to use.

_items.text: The student will need to find entirely new sources.
_items.feedback: Delayed logging risks losing detail about existing sources, not needing new ones.

_items.text: Nothing; the detail will still be there at the end of the week.
_items.feedback: Detail reconstructed from memory after several sources is exactly the risk being described.

_feedback.correct: Right. Delay risks misremembering or confusing the exact detail across several sources.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what happens to exact detail, like a page number, across several sources read in one sitting.
_incorrect.final: Delay risks misremembering or confusing detail between sources. Validity, needing new sources, and detail simply staying put are not the risk.

title: Check 3: what a record contains
displayTitle: In a piece of work for {{context}}, which of these belongs in a traceable source record?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What belongs in a traceable source record?

_items.text: The exact page or location the idea came from.
_items.feedback: Yes. The exact page or location is essential to a traceable record.

_items.text: The student's confidence in the source.
_items.feedback: Confidence in a source is not part of what makes a record traceable.

_items.text: How long the source took to read.
_items.feedback: Reading time has no bearing on tracing a source back to its detail.

_items.text: The font the source was printed in.
_items.feedback: Formatting detail like font is not part of a traceable record.

_feedback.correct: Yes. The exact page or location is essential; it is what makes the record traceable back to the idea's source.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what a reader would need to go and check the exact idea against its source.
_incorrect.final: The exact page or location is essential to a traceable record. Confidence, reading time, and font are not.

title: Activity: keeping the log running
displayTitle: Put these steps in order
body: These are the steps for keeping a source log running while gathering evidence. They are out of order.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the steps for keeping a source log running in the correct order.

_items.text: Open the log before starting a new research session.
Add each new source to the log the moment it is selected.
File the entry under a topic or source type as it is added.
Review the log at the end of the session to check nothing was missed.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order: open the log first, add each source as it is found, file it immediately, then review at the end.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. The log has to be open before anything can be added to it. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some steps are in the right place, but not all. Try again.

title: Activity: organised or not
displayTitle: Match each log to its outcome
body: Two ways of organising a source log, and what tends to happen when you need to find an entry again.
instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Match each way of organising a source log to its outcome.

_items.text: Every source is filed under the topic or claim it supports as soon as it is added.

_options.text: An entry can be found again quickly when needed.
Finding one entry means searching through everything.

_items.text: Sources are added to a single long list with no topic or type attached.

_options.text: An entry can be found again quickly when needed.
Finding one entry means searching through everything.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Filing by topic or claim keeps entries findable; an unfiled list does not.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what has to happen to find one entry in each case.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: One of these is right, but not both. Check the other.

title: Worked example: keeping the log usable
displayTitle: Worked example: keeping the log usable
body:
Two students each keep a source log while researching an assignment.

{{learner-a}} adds every source to a single long list in the order they were found, with no topic or type attached. Three weeks later, {{learner-a-pronoun}} cannot find the one source that covers a particular statistic without reading the whole list again.

{{learner-b}} files each source under the claim it supports as it is added, and checks each entry against the original the same day.

Only {{learner-b}}'s log can still be searched and trusted weeks later.

title: Activity: checking an entry against its source
displayTitle: Turn each card over
body: Four things to check an entry against its original source. Select a card to flip it and see why.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over.

back.body: If the entry includes a quote, is it word for word, not paraphrased by accident?
Does the page or location noted actually match where the idea appears in the source?
Do the author, year and title in the log match the source exactly?
Does the source actually say what the log entry claims it says?

title: Activity: ways to organise a source log
displayTitle: Ways to organise a source log
body: Four common ways of organising a source log. Open each to see it explained.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: By topic or claim
_items.body: Sources are grouped under the point in the assignment they support.

_items.title: By source type
_items.body: Books, journal articles and websites are grouped separately, since each needs different detail recorded.

_items.title: By date added
_items.body: Sources stay in the order they were found, useful for a short piece of work with few sources.

_items.title: By a combination
_items.body: Sources are filed by topic first, then by type within each topic, for a longer piece with many sources.

body: Run through this list regularly while researching a piece of work.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Every source is added to the log as it is selected, not afterward.

title: Check 1: keeping the log running
displayTitle: What keeps a source log useful while gathering evidence over several weeks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What keeps a source log useful over a long research period?

_items.text: Adding each source the moment it is selected, rather than reconstructing the list later.
_items.feedback: Yes. A log stays accurate when sources are added as they are found, not reconstructed from memory later.

_items.text: Waiting until the research is finished to build the log in one sitting.
_items.feedback: Building the log in one sitting risks exactly the memory problems logging as you go avoids.

_items.text: Keeping the log in a different format for every source type.
_items.feedback: Different formats are not what keeps a log useful; consistent, ongoing entry is.

_items.text: Only logging sources that are quoted directly.
_items.feedback: Every source used, quoted or not, needs an entry in the log.

_feedback.correct: Yes. Adding each source as it is found keeps the log accurate across a long research period.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what happens to detail when it is reconstructed from memory at the end.
_incorrect.final: Adding each source as it is selected keeps the log accurate. Waiting until the end, varying format, and quote-only logging do not.

title: Check 2: organising for findability
displayTitle: A source log holds forty entries in a single unsorted list. What problem does this create?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What problem does an unsorted source log create?

_items.text: Finding one specific entry again means searching through all forty.
_items.feedback: Right. Without filing by topic or type, finding one entry means checking the whole list.

_items.text: The sources stop being valid to cite.
_items.feedback: How a log is organised does not affect whether a source is valid to cite.

_items.text: The log automatically loses older entries.
_items.feedback: An unsorted list does not lose entries; it just makes them harder to find.

_items.text: Nothing; order of addition is organisation enough.
_items.feedback: Order of addition alone does not let a reader jump to a specific entry quickly.

_feedback.correct: Right. An unsorted list means searching through everything to find one entry.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what has to happen to find one entry among forty unsorted ones.
_incorrect.final: Finding one entry in an unsorted list of forty means searching all of them. Validity, losing entries, and order alone are not the issue.

title: Check 3: checking an entry
displayTitle: In a piece of work for {{context}}, a log entry claims a source found 'most students benefit', but the source actually says 'some students benefit'. What does checking the entry reveal?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does checking a log entry against its source reveal when the wording has drifted?

_items.text: The log entry overstates what the source actually says and needs correcting.
_items.feedback: Yes. Checking against the original catches exactly this kind of drift between the entry and the source.

_items.text: The source itself is unreliable.
_items.feedback: The mismatch is in how the log recorded the source, not in the source's reliability.

_items.text: The entry does not need a page number.
_items.feedback: Page numbers and wording accuracy are separate matters; this mismatch is about wording.

_items.text: Nothing; both versions mean roughly the same thing.
_items.feedback: 'Most' and 'some' make different claims; the log entry has overstated the source.

_feedback.correct: Yes. The entry overstates the source, which checking against the original is designed to catch.

_incorrect.notFinal: Compare exactly what the source says against exactly what the log entry claims.
_incorrect.final: The entry overstates the source: 'most' is not the same claim as 'some'. The source's reliability and page numbers are not the issue here.
